newsitem.title: USA: As Mir crew works, U.S. officials mull next mission.
newsitem.headline: As Mir crew works, U.S. officials mull next mission.

text.p: As Mir's crew worked to restore power to the space station on Tuesday, U.S. officials were mulling whether to keep sending astronauts to the troubled Russian craft.

"There's almost a constant, almost hourly conversation on Mir," Jeff Smith, a spokesman for White House science adviser Jack Gibbons, said by telephone. "Gibbons is doing daily memos to the president, sometimes twice a day."

Gibbons and members of Vice President Al Gore's staff were briefed on the shuttle-Mir program on Monday in a previously scheduled meeting, and an intensive, frequent dialogue on the safety issue is ongoing, Smith said.
U.S. astronaut David Wolf is scheduled to blast off for Mir on Sept. 25 aboard the space shuttle Atlantis, but whether he will actually embark on the station is still being debated.
Three separate U.S. inquiries into safety aboard Mir are proceeding, according to Michael Braukus of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.
Their findings will be taken into account at the final flight readiness review for the September shuttle mission. That review is expected to take place a week before the flight, Braukus said.

On Monday, the Russian station's main computer failed during a docking procedure, sending the craft into a 24-hour tumble and putting its solar panels out of alignment with the sun, prompting the station automatically to switch off all but vital life support systems.
The computer was fixed by Tuesday, but the solar panels were still not properly aligned.

It was the latest in a series of mishaps aboard the station, most notably a June 25 incident in which a space-going resupply ship punctured Mir's power-producing module, drastically cutting the station's energy supply.
Gibbons said last month that one key factor in deciding whether the next astronaut will fly on Mir is a restoration of power.

"If we're lucky, they think they can get maybe 30 to 50 percent of the power back; that would bring then Mir's power level up enough that we would be quite comfortable with continuation," Gibbons told reporters. "If they can't get the power up, then that's a real question."
For John Logsdon, a space policy expert at George Washington University, the essential question is whether sufficient function can be restored aboard Mir to allow scientific research.

"In my mind, it doesn't make sense to commit to a U.S. crew member unless you can do work and not just survive, and we'll know that in the next two or three weeks," Logsdon said in a telephone interview.
But even with its problems, safety has not reached a crisis point on Mir, Logsdon said: "It's not a good place to be right now; that's different than being in imminent threat of death."

Retired Adm. Richard Truly, a former astronaut who worked on the U.S.-Soviet Apollo-Soyuz mission in 1975 and later headed the inquiry into the 1986 Challenger disaster before becoming chief at NASA, voiced deep concern about Mir.
"I have been increasingly concerned about our involvement and the safety of the craft," Truly said by telephone from Golden, Colorado, where he directs the National Renewable Energy Laboratory.

"I can say that a fire aboard a spacecraft is not a yellow flag, that's a red flag," Truly said. "A problem with oxygen generation is not a yellow flag, it's a red flag. The crash of an unmanned vehicle into a space station is not a yellow flag, it's a red flag."
